title: Double at the End
kidRule: After a short vowel, a final F, L, S, or Z usually doubles. It happens in short words like JAZZ, and at the end of longer words too, like PRINCESS and WINDMILL. A few tiny words break the rule, like BUS, YES, and IF!
hint: Listen to the very last sound. It comes right after a short vowel, and that last letter does not like to be alone. What should you do?
reminder: After a short vowel, a final F, L, S, or Z is usually doubled. Write the last letter twice!

check.question: Why does PRINCESS end with two S's?
check.correctAnswer: Because a final F, L, S, or Z usually doubles after a short vowel!
distractors: Because every word that ends in S needs two of them
Because the second S makes the E say its name

words.def: The daughter of a king or queen.
words.sent: The princess rode a bicycle around the castle garden.
words.story: Queen Elizabeth II was still a princess when she trained as a truck driver and mechanic during World War II!
words.card: The *prince* and the *princess* raced their llamas around the moat!

words.def: A tall building with big sails that the wind turns to grind grain or pump water.
words.sent: The old windmill turned slowly in the breeze.
words.story: The Netherlands still has about 1,000 old windmills, and many of them were built to pump water off the land!
words.card: The *wind* spun the *windmill* so fast that it made everyone a milkshake!

words.def: A tool with a needle that always points north to help you find your way.
words.sent: The hikers used a compass to find the lake.
words.story: A compass needle is a tiny magnet, and it lines up with the Earth, which acts like one giant magnet!
words.card: Please *pass* the *compass*, this penguin is lost in the desert!

words.def: The house number, street, and town that tell where a place is.
words.sent: Write the address on the front of the envelope.
words.story: In the United States, ZIP codes were added to every address in 1963 to help sort the mail faster!
words.card: I mailed my fanciest *dress* to the wrong *address*, and now a goat is wearing it!

words.def: A strong building with thick walls made to keep enemies out.
words.sent: The children built a fortress out of couch cushions.
words.story: The Tower of London is a fortress that is more than 900 years old, and ravens still live there today!
words.card: Our pillow *fort* became a mighty *fortress* when the cat moved in as queen!

words.def: The top police officer of a county.
words.sent: The sheriff wore a shiny gold star on her vest.
words.story: This word comes from Old English words meaning 'shire reeve', the officer who looked after a shire, which is an old name for a county!
words.card: *She* is the *sheriff* of the sandbox, and no one may steal a bucket!

words.def: The thick, soft pad on a bed that you sleep on.
words.sent: The cat hid a toy mouse under the mattress.
words.story: This word comes from an Arabic word for a place where cushions are thrown down on the floor to sit or sleep on!
words.card: The elephant swapped her yoga *mat* for a bouncy *mattress*!

words.def: Tiny white flakes of dry skin that fall from the scalp.
words.sent: A special shampoo helped get rid of his dandruff.
words.story: Your skin is always making new cells, and you shed millions of tiny dead skin flakes every single day!
words.card: The snowman had *dandruff*, *and* everyone thought it was just more snow!

words.def: To make a wish, promise, or dream come true.
words.sent: She worked hard to fulfill her dream of becoming a pilot.
words.story: In Britain this word is usually spelled with just one L at the end, but in America it gets two!
words.card: To *fulfill* my wish, please *fill* the bathtub with jelly beans!

words.def: To make someone feel shy and red in the face in front of other people.
words.sent: Please do not embarrass me by singing in the store.
words.story: When you blush, tiny blood vessels in your cheeks open wider, and the extra blood turns your face red!
words.card: Do not *embarrass* the candy *bar* by telling everyone it melted!
